title: Add-on therapies
intro: Medicines and treatments sometimes used alongside gender-affirming hormone therapy to manage some of its effects. On testosterone: acne, scalp hair loss, periods that continue, and vaginal dryness. On oestrogen or androgen blockers: facial and body hair that remains, scalp hair, and changes in sexual function. None is hormone therapy in a different form, and none is automatic. It is background reading, not a prescription.

body: Hormone therapy changes more than the things someone is aiming for. Some effects come up often enough to have their own treatments. Each is possible rather than certain, and the medicines used for them are ordinary prescriptions, not hormone therapy in a different form [1][2].
Each medicine named here has its own page in the Medicines A–Z with doses, side effects and cost.

easy.text: Other medicines can help with some effects of hormone therapy.
For example: pimples, hair loss, periods, or dryness.
On oestrogen, some people want help with face hair, head hair or sex.
Ask your doctor which, if any, is right for you.

figure.caption: The effects of hormone therapy that are commonly treated, and what Australian guidance and product information name for each. Based on the Australian position statement, Australia's 2026 standards of care, the AJGP hormone therapy article and Australian product information [3][2][4][12][13].

body: These four sections are for people taking testosterone.

Acne on testosterone comes from the same mechanism as acne generally: androgens increase the size and output of the skin's oil (sebaceous) glands, and more oil means more breakouts on the face and body [5]. It tends to start within the first few weeks of treatment and is most active in the first one to two years, often settling after that even without treatment [4].

Australian guidance follows the usual escalation: a topical retinoid combined with benzoyl peroxide first, an oral tetracycline such as doxycycline if that is not enough, and isotretinoin — a stronger oral retinoid, usually managed with a dermatologist — for acne that is severe or scarring [4]. The three act at different points: the topical combination clears pores and reduces surface bacteria, doxycycline settles the inflammation that follows, and isotretinoin reduces the oil glands themselves, which is why it is kept for acne the other options have not controlled.

Testosterone is converted into dihydrotestosterone (DHT) by the enzyme 5-alpha reductase [6]. DHT drives most masculinising change, but its effect on hair follicles depends on where they sit: follicles on the beard, underarm and pubic area enlarge, while follicles at the temples, crown and front of the scalp tend to miniaturise — the same process behind male-pattern baldness [2]. It is slower to show than acne, typically taking over twelve months to become noticeable, and can continue for as long as testosterone does [2].

Topical minoxidil is a non-hormonal option; Australian product information is candid that exactly how it works is not known, though it appears to prolong the hair growth phase [7]. Finasteride instead blocks the enzyme that produces DHT in the scalp [6]. A small case review in trans men taking low-dose finasteride found modest improvement, without the sexual side effects reported in cisgender men on the same drug, though the evidence base remains limited [2]. It is contraindicated during pregnancy, relevant if a partner could become pregnant, and because it acts on the same pathway that drives masculinisation, some prescribers treat it as a trade-off to discuss rather than a routine add-on [2]. Hair loss can also take over a year to appear, so waiting before deciding on treatment is a reasonable choice [2].
list: Finasteride and dutasteride are not general blockers; they are commonly added for scalp hair loss, although Australian guidance notes it is unclear whether they add benefit [2]

body: Testosterone at gender-affirming doses does not reliably switch off ovulation, so periods can continue, especially in the first months of treatment [5]. On full-dose testosterone, periods are generally expected to stop within about six months, though this varies and not everyone reaches that point on testosterone alone; testosterone is not contraception regardless of whether periods have stopped [2].

If periods continue and cause distress, the options are reviewing whether the testosterone dose has reached target, an oral progestogen such as norethisterone or medroxyprogesterone acetate, or a levonorgestrel intrauterine device (IUD) [3]. Norethisterone is taken as tablets [8]; medroxyprogesterone acetate comes as tablets or as an injection given every three months [9]; the IUD is fitted once and can remain in place for several years [10]. The IUD and the three-monthly medroxyprogesterone injection also work as contraception; norethisterone and medroxyprogesterone tablets do not [2][8][9].

Testosterone suppresses the ovaries' own oestrogen production, and the vaginal lining depends on oestrogen to stay thick and lubricated. As that exposure drops, the tissue can thin and dry in a way similar to menopause, sometimes causing irritation, dryness or pain with penetration [5]. This tends to build up gradually over time on testosterone rather than appearing suddenly.

Low-dose vaginal oestrogen treats the tissue directly: daily for the first two weeks, then twice weekly, with product information describing systemic absorption as low enough that blood oestradiol stays within the usual postmenopausal range [11]. It acts locally and does not work against testosterone's effects elsewhere in the body [5]. Vaginal moisturisers, available without a prescription, are a non-hormonal alternative some people try first [2].

These three sections are for people taking oestrogen, an androgen blocker, or both. Micronised progesterone is part of feminising hormone therapy rather than an add-on; it is covered in the [doses guide](#/doses#sec-doses-3).

Oestrogen and androgen blockers lower the effect of testosterone on hair follicles, so facial and body hair usually grows more slowly. The change is gradual, with the largest effect after one to two years [16]. Hormones work on body hair more than on facial hair, and they cannot remove hair that has already grown, so many people also use hair removal [17][16].

Two androgen blockers used in Australia are also registered for unwanted hair growth (hirsutism) in women: spironolactone [12] and cyproterone acetate [13]. For someone already taking one as part of feminising therapy, it is already working on hair growth; it is not usually added a second time for hair.

Shaving, waxing and hair-removal creams are temporary. Laser hair removal and electrolysis give longer-lasting results but need several sessions [17]. They are procedures, not medicines, so they are not on the PBS, and Medicare has no item for hair removal; they are paid for privately, and Australian guidance describes them as costly [17][18]. If you take isotretinoin for acne, the product information advises avoiding waxing, dermabrasion and laser treatment during the course and for five to six months afterwards [14].
list: Body hair usually slows more than facial hair; the largest change is after one to two years [16][17]
Spironolactone and cyproterone are registered for unwanted hair growth in women, and are already part of many feminising regimens [12][13]
Laser and electrolysis: procedures, not prescriptions; no Medicare or PBS cover, so paid privately [17][18]
On isotretinoin, wait five to six months after the course before laser or waxing [14]
sections.note: Hormones keep slowing hair growth for one to two years, so ask your prescriber when it makes sense to start or plan hair removal [16].

body: Scalp hair loss of the male-pattern type is driven by dihydrotestosterone (DHT), which testosterone is converted into by the enzyme 5-alpha reductase [6][2]. Lowering testosterone with oestrogen and an androgen blocker removes much of that drive, so further loss often slows or stops, and Australian guidance notes that spironolactone and cyproterone have been shown to improve it [17][16].

Topical minoxidil is a non-hormonal option; Australian product information says exactly how it works is not known, though it appears to prolong the hair growth phase [7]. It can cause unwanted facial hair if it spreads from the scalp, so wash your hands well after applying it [7].

Finasteride and dutasteride block 5-alpha reductase. They are not general androgen blockers; they are commonly added for scalp hair loss, although Australian guidance notes it is unclear whether they add benefit [17]. Finasteride lowers PSA results by about half, so anyone who has prostate testing should tell the person ordering it [6]. The product information also lists depression, and loss of libido that can continue after stopping, among effects reported after marketing [6].
list: Feminising therapy itself often slows or stops scalp hair loss [17][16]
Minoxidil: non-hormonal; wash hands after use to avoid unwanted facial hair [7]
Finasteride or dutasteride: unclear added benefit on top of feminising therapy [17]
Finasteride halves PSA results; tell whoever orders a prostate test [6]
sections.note: Each of these medicines has its own page in the Medicines A–Z with doses, side effects and cost.

body: Reduced libido, fewer spontaneous erections and reduced erectile function are recognised effects of oestrogen and androgen blockers. Some people welcome these changes; for others they cause distress [15].

Australia's 2026 standards of care describe options such as lowering the dose of oestrogen or of the blocker, sildenafil or tadalafil (which help erections but not libido), and low-dose testosterone in some situations, each considered with your prescriber in light of your own goals [15]. The full list is on the [Related care and considerations](#/related-care#sec-related-care-1) page, in the section on sexual function.
list: Lower dose of the blocker or oestrogen; may bring back some masculinising effects [15]
Sildenafil or tadalafil: help erections, not libido [15]
Low-dose testosterone after orchidectomy or with full suppression, guided by blood tests; low-dose genital testosterone cream for penile pain, based on clinical experience [15]
